source: (authors not confirmed) (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Prompts built only from FrameNet frame definitions plus examples reach trained-parser level on role labeling with gold frames. Best prompted model 77.4 F1 vs trained parsers 75.6 to 77.1.
numbers: FSRL gold frames, 100 eval examples, 6 frames: DeepSeek Reasoner 77.4, Sonnet 3.5 76.3, GPT-4o 73.9, Haiku 3.5 68.9, GPT-4o Mini 67.1. Trained: Bastianelli 75.56 (FN1.5), Zheng 76.91, Ai and Tu 77.06 (FN1.7).
limits: Authors say direct comparison not feasible. Only 6 violence-related frames, tiny eval set, FrameNet version not stated.
agent_relevance: Frame text given in the prompt is enough for a strong model to fill roles. Supports writing the task as a frame with named roles in S1/S2.

source: (authors not confirmed) (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Showing the frame (definition and roles) to the model is the main driver. Zero-shot with no frame info collapses; with all frame info it recovers a lot; examples add more.
numbers: Full parsing, Killing frame: zero-shot no frame info 0.0 F1 for all four models; all frame info zero-shot 34.1 to 48.4; best-shot 68.7 to 82.9. Role labeling gold frame, no frame info vs all info zero-shot: GPT-4o Mini 3.9 vs 39.3; Sonnet 35.0 vs 39.1.
limits: Small gain from definition alone for some models (DeepSeek Chat 28.0 to 42.4). Single frame experiment.
agent_relevance: Naming roles explicitly is the ingredient. A schema step that lists roles for the task is supported.

source: (authors not confirmed) (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Rare or optional roles are the weak spot. Core participants are found well; Means, Instrument and Cause are not.
numbers: Killing frame per-role F1 best shots: Target 96 to 97; Victim 73 to 83; Killer 48 to 71; Cause 44 to 68; Means 0 to 50; Instrument 0 to 50 (GPT-4o Mini 0.0 on both).
limits: Roles with few training cases; strict exact-span scoring inflates errors.
agent_relevance: Empty-role detection (the S1/S2 goal) is the hard part for optional roles. Expect misses on non-core roles; add an explicit check pass.

source: (authors not confirmed) (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Errors compound across steps. Frame identification is easy (about 90 to 94 F1), but role labeling on predicted frames drops sharply for small models.
numbers: FI micro F1 90.5 to 94.3 across 6 models. FSRL on detected frames: Haiku 53.5, GPT-4o Mini 53.2, GPT-4o 66.9, Sonnet 68.6, Reasoner 74.9 (gold-frame values 67 to 77). Reasoner FI+FSRL 82.5.
limits: Each model feeds its own FI output into its own FSRL; no cross-model design.
agent_relevance: Cheaper models lose about 14 points when the frame is not given. Spend capability on frame choice or supply the frame by tool.

source: (authors not confirmed) (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: More examples help role labeling much more than frame naming; larger models beat smaller by about 5 to 7 points.
numbers: Shot gains: Exp 1 (Killing) +30 to +41 over zero-shot with frame info; Exp 2 FI +1.4 to +8.7. Best shot counts 50 to 400.
limits: Prompt length limits restrict how many frames fit at once.
agent_relevance: Frames ideal for few-shot use; long frame inventories do not fit, so retrieval of the right frame is needed.

source: Chundru et al. (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: A small open model prompted without training identifies FrameNet frames at 80 to 83 percent. Fine-tuning reaches the trained state of the art.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, mean of 3 runs. Direct-QA few-shot: 83.3 (FN1.5), 83.5 (FN1.7). Simple zero-shot 82.4 / 80.0. QA LoRA fine-tune 91.7 / 91.9. Best prior 92.5 / 92.6.
limits: Llama family mostly; English only; FrameNet inventory given in prompt.
agent_relevance: The model already knows frames. Prompting alone gets close but fine-tuning is needed for the last 9 points.

source: Chundru et al. (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: Frame names alone are weak zero-shot; lexical-unit definitions fix this. Frame names alone sometimes beat full definitions.
numbers: FN1.7 zero/few-shot: names only (Simple) 59.9 / 79.1; names plus LU definitions 76.5 / 80.9; Direct-QA with LU defs 80.8 / 83.5; adding frame definitions on top 81.7 / 82.8.
limits: Single model family for the ablation.
agent_relevance: More frame text is not always better. Short, targeted role/trigger cues can beat long definitions.

source: Chundru et al. (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: Definitions written by the model itself work as well as gold definitions, so frame knowledge is latent in the model.
numbers: FN1.7 zero/few-shot: gold definitions 78.4 / 79.3; GPT-4o-written 80.0 / 80.1; DeepSeek-V3.1 79.3 / 79.1; Llama-8B-written 75.0 / 75.4.
limits: Quality judged only through the downstream task; no human rating.
agent_relevance: The agent can generate its own frame definition at S1 and lose little. No external lexicon needed for common frames.

source: Chundru et al. (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: Out-of-domain frames are the weakness. Prompted model falls far on rare or artifact-related inputs; fine-tuning only part-way fixes it.
numbers: YAGS out of domain: zero-shot 65.4, FIDO 70.5, QA fine-tune 80.7. Artifacts set: zero-shot 25.6, fine-tune 49.6. Ambiguous targets 65.6 zero-shot, 69.7 few-shot.
limits: Some of these test sets have noisy labels.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a frame label for unusual domains. Keep a confidence note and an alternative frame.

source: Chundru et al. (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: Model errors overlap with the earlier trained parser: both fail on the same inputs.
numbers: FIDO 519 errors, Llama 538, 320 shared; 296 of 320 same wrong frame.
limits: Single comparison.
agent_relevance: Frame errors come from real ambiguity in the label set, so a second sample from the same model will not fix them.

source: Devasier et al. (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Prompted LLMs are poor at full argument identification. Fine-tuned small models beat them.
numbers: Frame element F1: few-shot GPT-4o-mini 0.471, DeepSeek V3 0.548, GPT-4o 0.592; fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini 0.768; Phi-4 0.785; Qwen2.5-72B 0.794 vs prior best 0.755 (Ai and Tu 2024).
limits: Input format matters; GPT-4o not fine-tuned (cost). Only FrameNet English.
agent_relevance: Open-ended role extraction from raw text without frame guidance is unreliable. Gold frame in the prompt matters (compare b01).

source: Devasier et al. (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Output format changes results a lot. JSON listing only the roles that exist is best.
numbers: Few-shot GPT-4o-mini F1: XML-tag 0.342; JSON-all 0.440; Markdown 0.448; JSON-exist 0.471.
limits: One model.
agent_relevance: Ask for only the roles that are present, in JSON. Listing all roles invites invented fillers.

source: Devasier et al. (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Fine-tuned models do not generalise to unseen roles. Unseen frame elements are the big drop.
numbers: Phi-4 F1: all test 0.785; unseen frames 0.708 (-7.7); unseen frame elements 0.515 (-27.0). Data: 1% 0.508, 25% 0.746, 100% 0.785. Out of domain YAGS: GPT-4o 0.387, Phi-4 0.533, SEMAFOR 0.570.
limits: YAGS labels may be noisy (authors own caveat).
agent_relevance: Roles that were not seen in the frame definition are lost. New task frames must be written out in the prompt, not left to memory.

source: Devasier et al. (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Frames can be picked by predicting the roles first. Role-based selection is strong on ambiguous words.
numbers: Phi-4 candidate method: 0.882 overall, 0.862 on ambiguous targets (0.894 with lexicon filter); CoFFTEA 0.926 overall. Size is not decisive: Qwen2.5-3B 0.752 beats Llama-3.3-70B 0.743.
limits: Random tie-breaking gives unstable multi-frame output; one seed.
agent_relevance: Test a frame by trying to fill its roles. A frame whose core roles cannot be filled is probably the wrong frame.

source: Evaluating the Impact of LLM-Assisted Annotation in a Perspectivized Setting: the Case of FrameNet Annotation
finding: A frame parser (LOME) used as pre-annotation raised frame coverage but did not speed up human work much. It misses unfilled core roles by design.
numbers: 311 sentences, 5 annotators. Annotation sets per doc: human 129, machine 126, machine plus human 160 (+24%). Unique frames per doc: 67.9 / 52.7 / 80.9. Core-role coverage: human 95.8%, machine 34.2%, machine plus human 90.7%. Time per sentence 14.96 vs 12.97 min.
limits: One parser, Brazilian Portuguese, annotators are co-authors, no gold accuracy or agreement reported.
agent_relevance: Machine output omits null-instantiated roles. A human or a second pass must ask which core roles are missing. This is the empty-role step the schema wants.

source: Rai, Croce, Basili (2026) Frame-Semantic Knowledge Injection for Event-Level Inference in LLMs
finding: Training Llama-3.1-8B on all 1,200+ FrameNet frames by LoRA improves natural language inference, especially entailment.
numbers: CONFER zero-shot 0.49 to 0.57 (+8). FrameNet-trigger subset (917): zero-shot Entailment 0.10 to 0.55; few-shot Neutral 0.74 to 0.88. SNLI diagnostic overall zero-shot 0.60 to 0.62, few-shot 0.73 to 0.77; few-shot Neutral falls 0.82 to 0.68.
limits: Gains small on SNLI; commonsense could explain some; no matched non-FrameNet LoRA control; rationales are manual post-hoc.
agent_relevance: Training is out of scope for our scaffold, but the Neutral-down trade-off warns that frame framing makes a model commit to a label more often.

source: Rai, Croce, Basili (2026) Frame-Semantic Knowledge Injection
finding: Zero-shot frame and role extraction by the frame-injected model rises but role spans stay low.
numbers: LU identification F1 0.50 to 0.62; frame prediction 0.66 to 0.81; roles only 0.17 to 0.34; roles plus exact span 0.11 to 0.20.
limits: Zero-shot over the full inventory; absolute scores modest.
agent_relevance: Even with frame training, exact role fillers are hard for an 8B model.

source: Steen, Reijnierse, Burgers (2014) When do natural language metaphors influence reasoning? Follow-up to Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2013)
finding: Four experiments found no difference between the beast and virus crime frames. Reading any crime text raised enforcement preference.
numbers: N analysed 253 (NL), 259, 252, 1026 (US MTurk). Frame effects F<1 to 1.10, all n.s. Exposure pre vs post: partial eta2 .14 and .28. Power for f=.25 about .95; for f=.10 only about .27.
quote: We do not find a metaphorical framing effect but instead show that there is another process
limits: Small effects undetectable at these Ns; 3 of 5 policy options favoured enforcement; one topic.
agent_relevance: Frame effects from a single metaphor word are small and easy to miss. Do not rely on one label word to steer the agent.

source: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2015) Measuring Effects of Metaphor in a Dynamic Opinion Landscape
finding: Re-coding with updated 2014 norms restores a small metaphor effect. The earlier null came from out-of-date coding of one option.
numbers: Pooled N=876 chi2(4)=16.35, p=.003, w=.14. Exp 1 N=526 w=.16; Exp 2 N=521 w=.09, p=.039. Reanalysis of Steen Exp 4 (N=350): virus frame B=-1.362, p=.036 under new norms; pooled p=.072.
limits: Effects small; Exp 2 marginal; MTurk; a coding error left 25.7% without the recall question; reanalysis is post hoc.
agent_relevance: The effect is real but small and depends on how outcomes are coded. Measure with fresh norms, not assumptions.

source: Holmes, Kassin, Flusberg (2024) When does suggestive language shape memory for car accidents? (Loftus and Palmer replication)
finding: Two large experiments (N=1204) did not replicate the smashed vs hit speed effect overall, matching earlier failures.
numbers: N=1204 across Exp 1a, 1b (400) and 2. No overall verb effect on speed estimates in any. Earlier null replications: Read et al. 1978, McAllister et al. 1988, Raghunath et al. 2021. Original paper cited over 3,400 times.
limits: Online samples, newer video, exploratory moderators.
agent_relevance: The best-known verb-framing demo is fragile. Do not build the agent on the claim that one verb shifts memory.

source: Holmes, Kassin, Flusberg (2024) Loftus and Palmer replication
finding: Moderators: people who wrote longer descriptions, or who judged smashed as only a little worse than hit, showed less framing. Pragmatic reading of the verb matters.
numbers: Description length x verb interaction b = -0.11 [-0.22, -0.004], p = .04 (mean 56 words, SD 32), replicated in Exp 2. Verb-severity difference moderated the effect.
limits: Exploratory analyses, borderline p.
agent_relevance: A richer own representation of the event shields against frame suggestion. Write out the scene in detail before accepting a leading label.

source: Holmes, Kassin, Flusberg (2024) Loftus and Palmer replication
finding: Boundary conditions found in older work: effect limited to unfamiliar settings and to some ages.
numbers: Read and Bruce (1984): only unfamiliar settings; Lipscomb et al. (1985): 7th and 8th graders but not younger children or college students; Goldschmied et al. (2017) conceptual replication inconclusive.
limits: Secondhand report of those studies.
agent_relevance: Frame effects are stronger when the person has weak knowledge. Agent should treat unfamiliar domains as high risk.

source: Zwaan (2026) Memory, Misinformation, and the Need to Replicate (blog on planned multi-lab Loftus and Palmer replication)
finding: As of late 2026 the effect has no modern large-scale replication. A multi-lab study of about 2000 is proposed but not run.
numbers: Planned N about 2000; a comment mentions an informal large replication that reportedly failed (no numbers given).
limits: Blog post, not a study; the informal failure is unverified.
agent_relevance: Treat the verb effect as unproven.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Many Labs 1, Asian disease framing, as cited in Investigating Variation in Replicability
finding: Multi-site replication of the gain-loss Asian disease framing found a smaller effect than the original.
numbers: Search snippet: 36 teams; replication effect about 53 to 67 percent of original size (99% CI). Secondary blog says significant in 31 of 36 labs.
limits: Not opened by me; numbers from search snippets only.
agent_relevance: Gain/loss wording effect is real but about 60 percent of the headline size.

source: Mandel (2014, 2015) on numeric quantifiers in framing problems, as cited by Westover (2025)
finding: A rival explanation: much of the classic framing effect comes from reading saved 200 as at least 200, so it is a pragmatic reading and not a change in the scene.
numbers: Cited claim: framing effects largely disappear once numeric quantifiers are interpreted in their linguistic context. No numbers given in this source.
limits: Second-hand citation; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Equivalent descriptions may not be equivalent in meaning. Check whether two frames really say the same thing before calling it bias.

source: Westover (2025) An analysis of AI Decision under Risk
finding: Five LLM configurations show gain-loss framing effects, but the sign flips across scenarios. Effects are large in a sports case and reversed in a career case.
numbers: 2,550 decisions, 25 runs per condition, risk 0 to 2. Championship: +1.40 to +1.84 (GPT-4o 1.84). Career transition: -0.37 to -0.60. Business merger -0.24 to +0.12. Geopolitical up to +0.64 (Claude Sonnet 4). Kappa 0.93.
limits: Coded by LLMs; table counts inconsistent; Gemini 2.5 excluded.
agent_relevance: Framing sensitivity of LLMs is scenario-dependent. Do not assume the sign. Test equivalent re-descriptions.

source: Lim, Kim, Whang (2026) DeFrame: Debiasing Large Language Models Against Framing Effects
finding: LLMs answer differently when the same content is worded in positive or negative terms. A 4-step prompt cuts the gap.
numbers: 8 models (3B to 14B). Framing disparity on BBQ disability ranges -4.3 to -41.4. DoNotAnswer-Framed (520 prompts) FD 0.9 to 5.4. DeFrame reduces BBQ framing disparity 92% and bias score 93% on average. Llama-3.1-8B ablation: BBQ disability FD -12.25 to 0.17; DoNotAnswer FD 3.08 to 1.67.
limits: Four LLM calls per question; binary framings only; 30 to 70B results only in appendix.
agent_relevance: Ask the model to restate the question in the opposite frame, then reconcile. Fits the guardrail against wording effects.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Debiasing prompts help framing-type biases but hurt others, so a generic be-unbiased line is not safe.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B. Judgment bias shifts -2.7 to -7.7 pp. Framing Effect accuracy 35.6% to 41.4% (+5.8) with debiasing; Illusion of Control +7.0; hyperbolic discounting -13.4; mental accounting and disposition effect worsen.
limits: Preprint, under review; framing is a small part of the benchmark; greedy decoding.
agent_relevance: Use targeted frame-reversal checks, not broad debias instructions.
